indeclinable (adverbial n. acc. sg. of द्रुत, past participle of √द्रु ‘to run’)

f. nom. sg. of असिपाशिन्; compound (see Samāsa); qualifies काली

sandhi.note: The t of कुटिलात् stays before t. -āḥ before the voiced l loses its visarga (तस्या ललाट…).
Final t becomes d before the voiced d.
ā + a → ā. The participle and the epithet are separate words: विनिष्क्रान्ता is the verb of the sentence, असिपाशिनी describes Kālī.

samasa.literal: crooked by the knitting of the brows
samasa.sense: the forehead furrowed in a frown

samasa.literal: from the board of the forehead
samasa.sense: from the flat of her brow
samasa.alt: As a rūpaka karmadhāraya, ललाटम् एव फलकम् ‘the forehead, a flat board’; the sense is the same.

samasa.vigraha: असिश्च पाशश्च असिपाशौ (itaretara dvandva); तौ अस्याः स्तः इति असिपाशिनी
samasa.type: itaretara dvandva with the possessive taddhita -in (fem. -inī)

morph.note: The kta participle of a verb of motion is active: ‘(she) came out’. निस् becomes निष् before k (s → ṣ after i inside the word).
A neuter accusative used as an adverb, the common way to make adverbs of manner: ‘quickly’.

mantras.anvaya: तस्याः भ्रुकुटीकुटिलात् ललाटफलकात् करालवदना असिपाशिनी काली द्रुतं विनिष्क्रान्ता।
mantras.anvaya_en: Source in the ablative (from her frowning forehead), subject with epithets (काली करालवदना असिपाशिनी), participle as verb.
mantras.lit: From the surface of her forehead, crooked with a frown, there swiftly came forth Kālī, of dreadful face, bearing sword and noose.
mantras.tr: From her forehead, knotted in a frown, there sprang at once Kālī, terrible of face, armed with sword and noose.

comm.t: Kālī is born from the Goddess’s frowning brow. This is a different event from 5.88, where Pārvatī herself turns dark and is called Kālikā after Ambikā has come out of her body; here Kālī comes out of Ambikā.

The Śākta tradition reads the sequence of 7.5–6 as anger taking form: the Devī’s wrath does not stay a mood but becomes a goddess who acts. Sword and noose are her first attributes; 7.7–8 complete the picture.
A modern reading: the fierce form does not come from outside the gracious one. The same Goddess who smiled in 7.3 frowns here, and what she sends out is still herself.

words.g: f. nom. sg.; compound (see Samāsa); qualifies Kālī (from 7.6)

words.g: f. nom. sg.; compound (see Samāsa)
f. nom. sg.; compound (see Samāsa)

words.g: f. nom. sg.; compound (see Samāsa)

sandhi.note: ā + a → ā: खट्वा ‘cot’ + अङ्ग ‘limb, leg’.
a + a → ā. Between the four words of this verse there is no sandhi: each ends in ā before a consonant.

samasa.vigraha: विचित्रं खट्वाङ्गं विचित्रखट्वाङ्गम् (karmadhāraya); विचित्रखट्वाङ्गं धरति इति
samasa.sense: carrying the khaṭvāṅga, a club shaped like the leg of a bedstead (traditionally topped with a skull)

samasa.vigraha: नराणां माला नरमाला (ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa); नरमाला विभूषणं यस्याः सा
samasa.literal: she whose ornament is a garland of men
samasa.sense: wearing a garland of human heads
samasa.alt: The text says only ‘garland of men’; the hymn of chapter 11 calls the same form शिरोमालाविभूषणा ‘adorned with a garland of heads’ (11.21), which fixes the sense.

samasa.vigraha: द्वीपिनः चर्म द्वीपिचर्म (ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa); द्वीपिचर्म परीधानं यस्याः सा
samasa.literal: she whose garment is the hide of a leopard
samasa.sense: clad in a leopard (or tiger) skin

samasa.vigraha: शुष्कं मांसं शुष्कमांसम् (karmadhāraya); अतिशयेन भैरवा अतिभैरवा; शुष्कमांसेन अतिभैरवा
samasa.sense: gaunt and fearsome, her flesh shrunk on her bones
samasa.alt: Also a bahuvrīhi, शुष्कं मांसं यस्याः सा, with अतिभैरवा as a separate idea (‘withered of flesh and most terrible’); the instrumental reading joins the two.

morph.note: परीधान is परिधान ‘garment’ with the prefix परि lengthened, a lengthening the language allows for prefixes before some nouns (compare परीहास). द्वीपिन् ‘leopard’ (literally ‘having island-like spots’) drops its n at the end of a compound member: द्वीपि-.

mantras.anvaya_en: No verb: four nominative epithets of Kālī, continuing 7.6.
mantras.lit: Bearing a strange khaṭvāṅga, ornamented with a garland of men, clothed in a leopard’s skin, exceedingly terrible with her dried flesh —
mantras.tr: She bore a strange skull-staff and wore a garland of human heads; a leopard’s hide was her garment, and her withered flesh made her more terrible still.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Skull-staff’ and ‘human heads’ give the traditional sense of खट्वाङ्ग and नरमाला; the verse has no verb, and ‘she bore … wore … was’ is supplied.

comm.t: The portrait of Kālī continues: weapon, ornament, garment, body. Every item belongs to the cremation ground and the ascetic who lives there.
Verses 7.6–8 are traditionally taken as the classic description of Kālī and Cāmuṇḍā, and they agree closely with the hymn’s address to Cāmuṇḍā in chapter 11 (11.21: दंष्ट्राकरालवदने शिरोमालाविभूषणे).

words.g: f. nom. sg.; compound (see Samāsa); qualifies Kālī

words.en: who filled the quarters with her roar
words.g: f. nom. sg.; compound (see Samāsa)

sandhi.note: The final k of दिश् (pausal दिक्) becomes the nasal ṅ before m. As in 7.7, the four words of the verse meet without sandhi.

samasa.vigraha: अतिशयितः विस्तारः यस्य तत् अतिविस्तारम्; अतिविस्तारं वदनं यस्याः सा
samasa.literal: she whose mouth has an excessive width

samasa.vigraha: जिह्वायाः ललनं जिह्वाललनम् (ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa); जिह्वाललनेन भीषणा
samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa
samasa.literal: terrifying through the lolling of the tongue
samasa.sense: her tongue hanging and swinging, a sight of terror

samasa.vigraha: निमग्ने च ते आरक्ते च निमग्नारक्ते (karmadhāraya of two adjectives); निमग्नारक्ते नयने यस्याः सा
samasa.literal: she whose eyes are sunken and red

samasa.vigraha: दिशां मुखानि दिङ्मुखानि (ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa); नादेन आपूरितानि दिङ्मुखानि यया सा
samasa.literal: she by whom the faces of the quarters are filled with a roar

morph.note: A bahuvrīhi whose relative pronoun is instrumental (यया ‘by whom’): the participle आपूरित (आ + √पॄ, causative ‘filled’) keeps its passive sense inside the compound.

mantras.anvaya_en: No verb: four more nominative epithets of Kālī, closing the description begun in 7.6.
mantras.lit: Having a very wide mouth, terrifying with the lolling of her tongue, having sunken red eyes, having the quarters filled with her roar —
mantras.tr: Her mouth gaped wide, her lolling tongue struck terror, her sunken eyes were red, and her roar filled every quarter of the sky.
mantras.tr_note: The epithets are turned into short clauses; nothing is added.

comm.t: The description ends with the mouth, the tongue, the eyes and the voice. The wide mouth is not ornament: it is how she will fight (7.9–13), swallowing the army whole.
The roar that fills the quarters answers the battle-cry of the Daityas. In chapter 8 Caṇḍikā will ask Kālī to open this same mouth wide (8.53: विस्तीर्णं वदनं कुरु) to drink the blood of Raktabīja.

√भक्ष् (curādi, 10 ‘to eat’), laṅ (imperfect), prathama-puruṣa ekavacana, ātmanepada
pronoun तद्, n. acc. sg.; qualifies बलम्
n. acc. sg. of बल; object of अभक्षयत

sandhi.note: Final t becomes d before the voiced b. The Gita Press prints the two words together here, but separately in 7.14 and 7.16 (तद् बलं); तत् is the demonstrative ‘that’, not a compound member.
ā + a → ā; likewise सुर + अरि → सुरारि.

samasa.sense: the mighty demons (महत् becomes महा- in such a compound)

samasa.literal: of the enemies of the gods

morph.note: Imperfect of the curādi stem भक्षय- with the ātmanepada ending -त. In 7.14 the same verb has the parasmaipada ending (अभक्षयत्); epic and Purāṇic Sanskrit uses both voices of this verb.
√हन् forms its causative from the stem घात- (घातयति ‘causes to be slain, kills’); -अन्ती is the feminine of the present participle.

mantras.anvaya: सा वेगेन अभिपतिता महासुरान् घातयन्ती तत्र सुरारीणां सैन्ये तत् बलम् अभक्षयत।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject सा with two participles (अभिपतिता, घातयन्ती); the main verb अभक्षयत with its object तत् बलम्; the locative सैन्ये … सुरारीणाम् gives where.
mantras.lit: She, having rushed with speed, slaying the great asuras, there in the army of the gods’ enemies devoured that force.
mantras.tr: She fell upon them with a rush, cutting down the great asuras, and there in the ranks of the gods’ enemies she devoured that host.

comm.t: Kālī’s first act is to charge into the army and eat it. The next four verses spell out how: elephants, horses, chariots and warriors go into her mouth.
Kālī devours what she fights; nothing of the enemy is left over. The tradition reads her mouth as the place where every form ends, which is why the same image returns with Raktabīja in chapter 8.

words.en: together with their rear-riders, goad-holding drivers, warriors and bells
words.g: m. acc. pl.; compound (see Samāsa); qualifies वारणान्
absolutive (lyap) of सम् + आ + √दा (juhotyādi, 3U; with आ ‘to take’)
m. instr. sg.; compound (see Samāsa)
n. loc. sg. of मुख; locative of destination
√क्षिप् (tudādi, 6P ‘to throw’), liṭ (perfect), prathama-puruṣa ekavacana, parasmaipada
m. acc. pl. of वारण; object of समादाय and चिक्षेप

samasa.vigraha: पार्ष्णिं गृह्णन्ति इति पार्ष्णिग्राहाः, अङ्कुशं गृह्णन्ति इति अङ्कुशग्राहिणः (both upapada tatpuruṣa); पार्ष्णिग्राहाश्च अङ्कुशग्राहिणश्च योधाश्च घण्टाश्च (itaretara dvandva); तैः समन्विताः, तान्
samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa containing an itaretara dvandva, whose first two members are upapada tatpuruṣas
samasa.literal: accompanied by heel-holders, goad-holders, warriors and bells
samasa.sense: war elephants with their whole crew and harness: the rear-rider, the mahout who drives with the hook (अङ्कुश), the fighting men and the bells; अङ्कुशग्राहिन् shortens to -ग्राहि inside the compound
the rider who guards the rear of the elephant
samasa.alt: In works on war पार्ष्णिग्राह is also the ally or force that guards (or attacks) the rear; with an elephant, the rear-rider is meant.

morph.note: With a prefix the absolutive takes -य (lyap) instead of -त्वा: सम् + आ + दा + य.
Perfect of √क्षिप्: reduplication चि- (kṣ → c), guṇa of the root vowel in the singular (क्षेप).
Verbs of throwing put the place into which something is thrown in the locative: मुखे चिक्षेप ‘threw into the mouth’.

mantras.anvaya_en: Absolutive (समादाय) then main verb (चिक्षेप), sharing the object वारणान् with its long qualifying compound.
mantras.lit: Seizing with one hand the elephants together with rear-riders, goad-holders, warriors and bells, she threw them into her mouth.
mantras.tr: Gathering up the war elephants in one hand, with their rear-riders, their drivers, their fighting men and their bells, she flung them into her mouth.

comm.t: The elephants, the first of the four arms of the army (7.2), go first — crew, harness and all, scooped up in a single hand.
A modern reading: the list is deliberately exhaustive. Nothing the asura army brings — its riders, its drivers, even its bells — is too large or too small to be taken in.
